result: The authors demonstrate that a single C-C mismatch enhances both DNA bendability and nucleosome mechanical stability for the 601 nucleosome positioning sequence. Using single-molecule FRET combined with optical trap force spectroscopy, they show increased unwrapping forces for mismatches at three positions (R18, R39, R56) in the nucleosome, with mismatch-containing nucleosomes showing different behaviors between stretching cycles compared to unmodified nucleosomes.
evaluation: All reviewers explicitly affirm these core findings. Reviewer 1 states the manuscript 'reports important data' with 'compelling evidence obtained by single-molecule FRET experiments' showing mismatches lead to more stable nucleosomes. Reviewers 2 and 3 confirm the authors 'found that unwrapping becomes slower when CC is introduced at three different positions' and that 'a CC mismatch enhances nucleosome mechanical stability.' The reviewing editor notes 'the authors addressed the points in the reviews.'

result: The authors show that the mismatch-induced change in local flexibility has a strengthening effect only on the side containing the mismatch (ED1 side), as demonstrated by comparing ED1 and ED2 labeling patterns where the ED2 side showed nearly the same unwrapping pattern as the control 601 nucleosome.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly confirms 'the CC mismatch only affects the local unwrapping dynamics of the outer turn of nucleosomal DNA,' supporting the claim that the effect is localized to the mismatch-containing side. No reviewer challenges this finding, and the data interpretation is accepted without critique.

result: Using single-molecule DNA cyclization assays, the authors demonstrate that C-C mismatches increase DNA bendability, with a ~sevenfold increase in cyclization rate and reduced looping times at all three tested positions. Control experiments with different biotin tether positions confirm this is not an artifact of the experimental setup.
evaluation: Reviewers 2 and 3 both explicitly confirm the authors 'confirmed that CC is the most flexible mismatch using the FRET-based cyclization assay' and that 'it is confirmed with a single-molecule cyclization essay that the introduction of a CC mismatch increases the flexibility of a DNA fragment.' No concerns are raised about the cyclization data or controls.

result: The authors tested multiple mismatch types and found that C-containing mismatches (C-C, C-A, C-T) showed the largest reduction in looping times, while G-containing mismatches (G-G, G-T, G-A) had little to no effect on DNA bendability.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly notes that the authors' findings 'correlate with the results from DNA buckling assays reported by Euler's group (NAR 41, 2013) using the same mismatches as an orthogonal way to measure DNA kinking,' providing independent validation. No reviewer questions these comparative mismatch results.

result: The authors demonstrate species-specific differences in nucleosome mechanics, showing that yeast nucleosomes are mechanically less stable and more symmetrical in outer turn unwrapping compared to Xenopus nucleosomes, with different FRET values and force-unwrapping profiles.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly confirms 'intriguingly, asymmetric unwrapping was more pronounced for yeast histones' and Reviewer 3 notes 'yeast and Xenopus histones show different behaviors in this assay.' The reviewing editor's note that authors addressed reviewer points suggests any concerns were resolved.

result: The authors propose that reduced nucleosomal DNA accessibility due to mismatch-enhanced mechanical stability could explain the preferred accumulation of single-nucleotide substitutions in the nucleosome core, potentially hindering mismatch repair machinery access.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly states 'the biological significance and implications of the findings remain unclear,' directly questioning this interpretive claim. Reviewer 3 notes the authors 'discuss that substitution rates are higher towards the middle of the nucleosome' but does not affirm the mechanistic connection. The model is presented but its biological relevance is questioned.

result: The authors interpret their findings in the context of DNA flexibility-nucleosome stability relationships, showing that mismatches can symmetrize DNA flexibility but do not have a global effect on coordination of unwrapping of the two DNA ends, unlike flexibility achieved through sequence elements.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 notes this work 'appears to be a sequel to this line of projects' and confirms the authors 'observed that force-induced unwrapping happens more slowly for DNA that is more bendable because of changes in sequence or chemical modification,' affirming consistency with previous findings. The interpretation is accepted without challenge.

result: The authors discuss that species-specific differences in nucleosome mechanics may be explained by histone sequence divergence and structural differences, with yeast H3 being less capable of wrapping DNA tightly, and suggest that DNA-to-nucleosome mechanics translation depends on histone sequence and post-translational modifications.
evaluation: These interpretive claims about species differences are supported by the experimental data on yeast vs. Xenopus nucleosomes that reviewers explicitly affirmed. No reviewer challenges the structural/sequence-based explanations, and the reviewing editor notes authors made 'appropriate text additions and clarifications.'

result: The authors discuss limitations and broader implications, noting that most mismatches may be repaired before nucleosome deposition, that their findings may be most relevant for rare cases or non-replicative mismatches, and predict that other DNA lesions affecting flexibility would similarly alter nucleosome stability.
evaluation: These discussion points represent appropriate caveats and predictions that reviewers did not challenge. The reviewing editor's note that authors made 'appropriate text additions and clarifications' suggests these nuanced discussion points were added or refined in response to review, and were accepted.
